Its purpose is to allow the public access to the rich resources available at UT regarding the collection of donated nineteenth and twentieth-century Navajo rugs. This site aims to be a resource for educators, students, and researchers by hosting a repository of digital collections, contextualizing blog posts, lesson plans, classroom activities,  and a platform for respectful collaboration and discourse. That being said, it should also become a place for conversations around decolonizing the archive, and the long-lasting effects of American colonization of Native land. I have intentionally chosen to frame this site around the Navajo and their creations in an effort to recenter the discussion of their culture and commodity production around them. While collectors and traders are described, the true purpose of this project is to diversify conversations about Navajo textiles to include them. item.title: The Navajo
item.dc:creator: alinaisabella
item.content:encoded:
"Spider Woman instructed the Navajo women how to weave on a loom which Spider Man told them how to make. The cross poles were made of sky and earth cords, the warp sticks of sun rays, the healds of rock crystal and sheet lightning. The pattern was a sun halo, white shell made the comb. There were four spindles: one a stick of zigzag lightning with a whorl of cannel coal; one a stick of flash lightning with a whorl of turquoise; a third had a stick of sheet lightning with a whorl of abalone; a rain streamer formed the stick of the fourth, and its whorl was white shell." (Navajo Legend)

Information provided by Navajo Nation and discovernavajo.com.

Introduction

The Navajo Nation extends into the states of Utah , Arizona and New Mexico, covering over 27,000 square miles of unparalleled beauty. Diné Bikéyah, or Navajoland, is larger than 10 of the 50 states in America.

Visitors from around the world are intrigued and mystified when they hear the Navajo language – so, too, were the enemy during World War II. Unknown to many, the Navajo language was used to create a secret code to battle the Japanese. Navajo men were selected to create codes and serve on the front line to overcome and deceive those on the other side of the battlefield. Today, these men are recognized as the famous Navajo Code Talkers, who exemplify the unequaled bravery and patriotism of the Navajo people.

Navajo Nation Government

Today, the Navajo Nation is striving to sustain a viable economy for an ever increasing population that now surpasses 250,000. In years past, Navajoland often appeared to be little more than a desolate section of the Southwest, but it was only a matter of time before the Navajo Nation became known as a wealthy nation in a world of its own. The discovery of oil on Navajoland in the early 1920's promoted the need for a more systematic form of government.

In 1923, a tribal government was established to help meet the increasing desires of American oil companies to lease Navajoland for exploration. Navajo government has evolved into the largest and most sophisticated form of American Indian government. The Navajo Nation Council Chambers hosts 88 council delegates representing 110 Navajo Nation chapters.

See the Navajo Nation government in action as the 88 Council delegates (representing 110 Navajo Nation chapters, or communities) discuss critical issues and enact legislation to determine the future of the Navajo people. Reorganized in 1991 to form a three-branch system (executive, legislative and judicial), the Navajos conduct what is considered to be the most sophisticated form of Indian government. While the Council is in session, you'll likely hear delegates carry on the tradition of speaking in Navajo, providing a perfect example of how the Navajo Nation retains its valuable cultural heritage while forging ahead with modern progress. When the Council is not in session, legislative work is done by 12 “standing committees” of the Council. Inside the circular Council Chambers, the walls are adorned with colorful murals that depict the history of the Navajo people and the Navajo way of life. For more info about tours, call 928-871-6417 or write to P.O. Box 1400 , Window Rock, AZ 86515.

Navajo Code Talkers

Navajo Code Talkers At Iwo Jima, Major Howard Connor, 5th Marine Division signal officer, declared, "Were it not for the Navajos, the Marines would never have taken Iwo Jima." Connor had six Navajo code talkers working around the clock during the first two days of the battle. Those six sent and received over 800 messages, all without error.

[caption id="attachment_657" align="alignleft" width="430"] Navajo Indian communication men with the Marines on Saipan landed with the first assault waves to his the beach. (NARA via Wikimedia Commons)[/caption]

In May 1942, the first 29 Navajo recruits attended boot camp. Then, at Camp Pendleton , Oceanside , California , this first group created the Navajo code. They developed a dictionary and numerous words for military terms. The dictionary and all code words had to be memorized during training. Navajos could encode, transmit, and decode a three-line English message in 20 seconds. Machines of the time required 30 minutes to perform the same job. Approximately 400 Navajos were trained as code talkers.

Guadalcanal, Tarawa, Peleliu, Iwo Jima : the Navajo code talkers took part in every assault the U.S. Marines conducted in the Pacific from 1942 to 1945. They served in all six Marine divisions, Marine Raider battalions and Marine parachute units, transmitting messages by telephone and radio in their native language -- a code that the Japanese never broke. Long unrecognized because of the continued value of their language as a security classified code, the Navajo code talkers of World War II were honored for their contributions to defense on Sept. 17, 1992, at the Pentagon, Washington, D.C. Excerpts taken from a Fact Sheet prepared by the Navy & Marine Corps WWII Commemorative Committee.

Flag
The Navajo Nation Flag, designed by Jay R. Degroat, a Navajo from Mariano Lake, New Mexico, was selected from 140 entries, and was officially adopted by the Navajo Nation Council on May 21, 1968 by Resolution CMY-55-68. [caption id="attachment_659" align="alignright" width="367"] Navajo Nation Flag[/caption]

On a tan background, the outline of the present Nation is shown in copper color with the original 1868 Treaty Reservation in Dark Brown. At the cardinal points in the tan field are the four sacred mountains. A rainbow symbolizing Navajo sovereignty arches over the Nation and the sacred mountains. In the center of the Nation, a circular symbol depicts the sun above two green stalks of corn, which surrounds three animals representing the Navajo livestock economy, and a traditional hogan and modern home. Between the hogan and the house is an oil derrick symbolizing the resource potential of the Tribe, and above this are representations of the wild fauna of the Nation. At the top near the sun, the modern sawmill symbolizes the progress and industry characteristic of the Navajo Nation's economic development.

The small park near the Navajo Nation Administration Center features the graceful redstone arch for which the capital is named. The Navajo Nation headquarters and other government offices were built in close proximity to this mystical rock formation.

[caption id="attachment_660" align="alignright" width="447"] Navajo Memorial Park, Window Rock, Navajo Nation (Jeff Brunton via Wikimedia Commons)[/caption]

More recently, the Navajos have built a Veteran's Memorial at the base of Window Rock to honor the many Navajos who served in the U.S. military. Many Navajo soldiers are recognized in the annals of history for their role as Code Talkers, whereby they used the native language to create a code that was never broken by the enemy. Historians credit the Navajo Code Talkers for helping to win World War II. The park has many symbolic structures: a circular path outlining the four cardinal directions, 16 angled steel pillars with the names of war veterans, and a healing sanctuary that is used for reflection and solitude that features a fountain made of sandstone. Open daily from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. For more info call 928-871-6647 or write to Navajo Nation Parks & Recreation Dept., P.O. Box 9000 , Window Rock, AZ 86515

item.title: Project History
item.dc:creator: alinaisabella
item.content:encoded:
began as the final project for a graduate level Public and Digital History course at the University of Texas at Austin under Dr. Joan Neuberger. The mission of “Woven into History” is to allow the public access to the rich resources available at UT regarding the collection of donated nineteenth and twentieth-century Navajo rugs. This site aims to be a resource for educators, students, and researchers by hosting a repository of digital collections, contextualizing blog posts, lesson plans, classroom activities,  and a platform for respectful collaboration and discourse.I have intentionally chosen to frame this site around the Navajo and their creations in an effort to recenter the discussion of Navajo culture and commodity production to include. While collectors and traders are described, they are not the focus of this site. However, I am aware the contents of this site reveal more about the archival process and the collector, F.A. Williams, than they do the creators of the beautiful, creative works present. Much is yet to be done to deconstruct the impact of the colonial nature of the archive on indigenous peoples, but I hope this is a step in the right direction.
Method
  • Photos of textiles were used with the permission of the Art and Art History department and downloaded from the DASe  (Digital Archive Service) in the Art & Art History Visual Resources Collection.   Additional textiles in this UT hidden collection are available to view with a UT eid. Simply search "textiles" or "southwestern Native American" to view the entire list of digitized holdings.
  • Digitized paper records can be found in the Art and Art History Collection. Contact me or Dr. Astrid Runggaldier for further information.
  • Images are claimed fair use as they are antique postcards if not otherwise noted.

item.title: Turkey Red and the Making of an Oriental-Navajo Rug
item.dc:creator: alinaisabella
item.content:encoded: The late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries witnessed a boom in the lucrative rug trade, the formations of which began much earlier. Although technological developments made rug and carpet production more inexpensive and accessible, handmade Navajo and Oriental rugs were still in high demand. By utilizing the catalogs, analyses and reports of traders and rug experts in the early twentieth century American southwest, this paper will discuss the theories that might suggest a relationship between Turkish and Navajo rugs. Further, the trader and expert records will be used to compare references to both groups. In this paper, I ask how traders understood the relationship between Oriental and Navajo rugs, if  there is any empirical evidence in these accounts to suggest a relationship or influence, how religious ideologies shape the way traders marketed these rugs, and, finally, if there is any truth to a connection between Islamic prayer rugs and Navajo textiles.

item.title: Bedouins of the Great Southwestern Desert
item.dc:creator: alinaisabella
item.content:encoded:
A Dine´ (Navajo) weaver sits beneath her loom, positioning herself at the heart of a tradition. Day in and day out she works toward a Chief’s blanket which is roughly 5.25 x 4.25 feet. The loom is much larger than that. She has imagined the design already- nine crosses spread evenly along the width and center, lines of varying size alongside them. Bold blues, reds, and greens are stitched and cross stitched. When it is completed, the blanket will represent a long history of weaving in the plains, by Navajo, Pueblo and other indigenous groups. [caption id="attachment_799" align="aligncenter" width="546"] Chief’s Shoulder Blanket: 1074-106[/caption] Weavers developed a series of socioeconomic ties to manufacturers, traders, collectors and other U.S. consumers that exported the practice of weaving beyond the American Southwest and resulted in the commodification of Native textiles. One key example of this is the Chief’s blanket- yes, like the one on Antiques Roadshow. The Chief’s blanket is key in the commodification of Diné textiles.  The vivid colors, mostly reds, and blues are some of the Chief’s blanket’s most noticeable and highly valued identifiers. This blog will discuss on microhistory of the bright red dye, and the ways it was transformed to increase what traders felt they could sell it for. The weaving style of Chief’s blankets is categorized into three phases. The first phase lasted until about 1865 when Navajo blankets typically were made with stylistically simple patterns with mostly brown and blue stripes. The second phase, which occurred between 1850 and 1880, included a larger array of design elements and colors, like rectangles, reds, and greens. The third phase of what is referred to as the classical period occurs between about 1880 and the end of the century. In blankets of this period, bright reds were accompanied by diamonds and geometrical motifs. One of the key features of the Chief’s blanket is the consistency of the red. However, early traders catalogs, magazines and newspapers suggest controversy method manufacturers used to create the bright and unwavering red in the third phase of Navajo rug production. [caption id="attachment_910" align="alignleft" width="285"] Tincture of the root or Dyer's Madder (NYPL)[/caption] Turkey Red Textile and weaving experts suggest the first type of red dye introduced into European weaving originated in Turkey, thus the name “Turkey Red”. According to Barbara Brackman, “in the 1750s the secret of Turkey red dyeing was leaked to the European continent where French and English mills began producing Turkey red plain and print cottons.” This process was so lengthy and complex, the final Turkey Red product was often three times the cost of quicker, industrialized red dyes. This process was so complex, it was highly valued. Such margins provided ample encouragement for European weavers to utilize alternate methods of dying, like the one originating from madder root, or in the case of some American traders, fabricate a connection to Turkey Red with a new, simpler, and cheaper American element. Bayeta (Balleta) [caption id="attachment_106" align="alignright" width="340"] Mexican Indian Collecting Cochineal with a Deer Tail by José Antonio de Alzate y Ramírez (1777)[/caption] Europeans soon realized - thanks to indigenous knowledge- a bright red could also be extracted from a cheaper, more accessible set of ingredients. The cochineal beetle- which makes its home on a cactus-  can produce vivid bayeta dyes. Bayeta dye-making is believed to have originated in Latin America and Mexico. Once discovered by Europeans, colonists exported the cochineal beetle and its carminic acid to be shipped across the Atlantic, and later, to Germantown, Pennsylvania to be converted and resewn into a variety of colors. Like the madder dye, bayeta was long-lasting and its garments garnered significant value. However, they cost close to nothing to make. Seeing an opportunity to further market their products, some traders stepped in.  Traders' sales catalogs and magazines of the Southwest often included photographs of Navajo textiles and descriptions of blankets and rugs made with Turkey Red! However, we have established that the original method of producing turkey red- the madder root- was only available in Europe, and that could not explain the red in western indigenous textiles long before the arrival of Europeans. Were traders intentionally deceptive to customers by drawing a connection between bayeta dyes and turkey red? Or, were there cultural and historical factors traders believed to be true, such as a possible connection between the Navajo and the Orient, that could also be marketed? Also, why were traders so quick to establish the quality of bayeta over mechanized dyes, while simultaneously connect it to Turkish products?  They simply had a product to sell. There seemed to be contention between a supposedly handmade bayeta blanket and another more mechanized dyed cloth made in Germantown.  Charles Avery Amsden wrote that dye made in “Germantown [which had] a wooly and soft rather than a silky, hard, and rough feel.” Though the efficiency of mechanization would force bayeta to be replaced by the mechanized the Germantown-made dye at the end of the nineteenth century, according to James, it did not compare in quality to bayeta. Even as it became less efficient to use bayeta, it served business to highlight more expensive and higher quality elements of the weaving process.  Such associations were intentionally drawn by traders to increase the sales value of the textiles. Though the processes differed, many believed this dye, despite its American origins, had if not material, symbolic connections to the Orient. Charles Lummis, in an 1898 column on Navajo rugs says, “This red material is from a fine Turkish woolen cloth called balleta. It used to be imported to Mexico, whence the Navahos [sic.] procured it at first...The Navahos used to ravel this cloth and use the thread for their finest blankets; and it made such blankets as never have been produced elsewhere.”  In the chapter of Navaho Weaving called “Bayeta--1800-1863”, Amsden openly addresses the inaccuracies of Lummis’s column:  
The romanticists are fond of telling too that bayeta was a Spanish fabric. Lummis (who was never found tamely plodding in another’s track) rose to yet greater heights and derived if from distant Turkey (1896) for no stated reason.
Amsden goes on to admit much of the earliest bounds of bayeta transported to the southwest were taken there through the Spanish in Mexico, the result of which was  “a considerable leaven of European influence came into the native culture of the Southwest and found in varying degrees a permanent place therein.”  On one hand, Amsden castigates Lummis for drawing too strong a connection between the Navajo and the Orient, and on the other, he expresses a profound European influence on the Navajo weaving culture. One is left to wonder who Amsden believed influenced European weaving practices. Nevertheless, this conflation of the two dying methods is a normative quality of nineteenth and early twentieth- century writings about Navajo textiles. The trader’s history of dyes was used to both increase the value of the product, and add character to a seemingly obscure element of the weaving process. By the early 20th century, despite technological developments making mass-produced textiles more inexpensive and accessible, handmade Navajo and Oriental rugs were still in high demand. The narratives expressed by Brackman, Amsden, Lummis, and others reflect the intention of traders and Southwestern specialists to paint a however fictitious correlation between the Orient and Native weavers. Although technological developments made mass-produced rug and carpet production more inexpensive and accessible, handmade Navajo and Oriental rugs were still in high demand. The bayeta dye sometimes referred to as “Turkey Red” was just one element of the process of weaving commodified and marketed to paint an ever-alluring image of the Great American Desert that connected it to a distant and very different Middle Eastern desert, or as J.B. Moore unabashedly writes, “these Bedouins of the great Southwestern Desert”. -------- Woven into History hosts several blankets made with both bayeta and “Germantown” dyes including:

item.title: Space, Place, and Manifest Destiny
item.dc:creator: alinaisabella
item.content:encoded:
The goal of this lesson is to discuss the impact of western expansion and manifest destiny on Native peoples in the American Southwest. I will include excerpts from Dreaming of Sheep in Navajo Country and Misplaced Massacre. An alternate lesson plan will touch on the interconnectedness of western expansion and the Civil War.
Reading:
Primary Sources
  • One of Linked Trader Catalogs
  • Selected Acquisition records
  • One blanket/rug
Secondary Sources
  • Marsha Weisiger, Dreaming of Sheep in Navajo Country (p. 3-30)
  • Erika Bsumek. Indian-Made: Navajo Culture in the Marketplace, 1868-1940.
Exercise:
Utilizing the acquisition records, linked trader catalogs and students will be required to think deeply on biases, national identity, and systematic and environmental racism.

item.title: Trader Catalogs, Weaver Profiles, and Selling Experience
item.dc:creator: alinaisabella
item.content:encoded:
“Pray to it and talk to it,’that is what my mother says to me… I hear her praying in the morning to her loom.” Mary J. Barker, Wide Ruins, Arizona
Dine´ (Navajo) weavers traced their craft to Spider Woman. Spider-woman is said to have been the first to use the loom and wool, which she consequently gave to the Dine´ to do for themselves. Centuries later, weavers felt the process of weaving not only connected them to their ancestors, but to deities.  This creation was important and deeply personal. That did not hinder some elements crucial to the weaving process, like dyes and yarn, from evolving to accommodate the demand for rugs for American clients through trader middle-men. By end of the 19th century,  Dine´ women weavers felt their craft could be both spiritual and profitable in the US marketplace.
“ I usually talk to the people I sell my rug to; make sure it’s going to a good home and they’re going to take care of it. I guess it’s like a baby- you put all that work into it, take care of its problems- you want someone who is going to appreciate it”
Lenora Davis, Ganado, Arizona
There was a divide between how traders understood their relationship with weavers and how they portrayed them in catalogs. Traders often featured profiles of Navajo weavers in their catalogs to emphasize that the blankets they produced were handmade. As commercial rug manufacturing challenged the trader’s monopoly on the market for rugs, traders worked to disrupt the market for machine-made goods by touting the “primitive” nature of both rugs and weavers. Traders that the handmade goods made by weavers were unique. While traders emphasized that the goods Navajo weavers made were unique, they often cast the weavers themselves as fitting the broad stereotype of passive actors in the marketplace. Yet, the actions of weavers reveal that were savvy about the market and conscious of traders’ various tactics of exploitation and underpayment. Evidence illustrates that they demanded respect and fair treatment. This came in the form of acknowledging unfair sales, but also, in refusal to produce specific designs. There was a variety of ways weavers attempted to accommodate the demands for their textiles. Some chose to use the designs while others did not. (See Bsumek, 42 for letter from Louisa Alcott to Lorenzo Hubbell Jr.). The popularity of trader catalogs, where consumers could select preferred patterns before purchase, occupied a very distinct moment in American history. This occurred against the backdrop of an expanding consumerist society, immediate access to ethnic products, the reemergence of the Southwest in defining American cultural identity, and the willingness of women weavers to transition from the creation of solely cultural outerwear to a broader consuming public wanting to purchase rugs and carpets. (See lesson plan on teaching the market revolution). While it might sound familiar to an audience with Amazon prime and large retail stores, this was a revolutionary moment. How did the cultural legacy of Navajo weaving become another product to be consumed?     [gallery type="columns" size="full" link="none" ids="480,481,482,483"] Traders felt even this spiritual element of the weaving process could be commodified and used to contest the mass production of inexpensive textiles. Traders would sell quality and personality to justify pricing. The men who traded Navajo women’s creations highlighted the individuality of each rug and each weaver in their widely distributed catalogs. J. B. Moore, for example, was known to include names and portraits of each weaver with the final product. In the photos above, it is clear traders emphasized the importance of the loom by photographing individual weavers in front of it. While the weavers appear small in the photograph, their products loom large in the marketplace. [caption id="attachment_479" align="alignright" width="258"] Photo of "Bi-leen Al-pai-Bi-zha-ahd" by Sim Schwemberger in John Bradford Moore's "The Navajo".[/caption] One such weaver was “Bi-leen Al-pai-Bi-zha-ahd” (right) whose name was spelled out syllabically in order for the owner of the blanket to be able to properly pronounce her name. According to Moore, she specialized in rugs that mirrored Oriental ones yet she never duplicated a design and was “the Navajo weaver who set the standard of excellence at once the admiration and despair of all other weavers”. Seeing that traders often attempted to persuade weavers to incorporate designs and motifs they felt held greater value in the market (see J.B. Moore's catalog). The catalogs, however, neglected the personhood of the weaver and her resistance. By coupling this narrative with other images of Dine´ women sitting at the base of their looms (above) Moore strips the Bileen Alpai Bizhaahd’s motivations for weaving, ownership of the textile, and creativity from the narrative, replacing them with what she represents: an antique, a far removed memory of the underdeveloped Southwest. Moore’s catalog exchanges her refusal to weave his designs into her creations, with an individuality suitable for the capitalistic consumers that laid the groundwork for the catalogs in the first place.    
“They used to pass out the papers and say: ‘you weave one like this.’... Grandmother that passed away, she never did copy one.  She didn’t want the paper. She used to say: ‘I’ll weave my own pattern’.”
Mikes Daughter Frank, Jedito, Arizona
  It is also important to discuss the mutually beneficial, if not entirely fair, relationship between Navajo people and traders living among them. To conclude the catalog, Moore writes: “Our first thought of course is to get them to weaver for us and for us only, all the fine rugs they possibly can, and then find a buyer for these. But it is also our mission to buy any and everything the Navajo has to sell...any and everything he has which he wants to turn to cash...And it is also our purpose to sell him in turn, all his supplies, groceries, dried goods, clothing...everything in fact that he has need for and the money to buy with.”The result was an imbalance of power and unequal dependence of Navajo on the trader. Women were aware of this, often in letters and in person, calling attention to the exploitative nature of the relationship, and expecting more. The early practice of weaving was very much linked to cultural ceremonies and practicality- the need for warm outerwear produced a shoulder blanket for colder days, a saddle blanket to be placed on the backs of horses, and the like. Rarely were they used as rugs and carpets.  (Designs and dyes were also deeply symbolic: Bedouins of the Great Southwestern Desert: Imagining a Connection between the Dine and The Orient). While traders like Moore and Hubbell often speculated as to the religious or emotional significance of designs and patterns, they were often inaccurate. Their records provide a suitable example of how to think critically about the trader archive.  The best way to reflect on these narratives is to firstly decolonize the existing narrative, and secondly, return to the source of these stories: Navajo women. In an effort to do so, I would invite you to watch an interview with Sadie Curtis in 2006, told in her own language, with her own words describing her journey to weaving. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Hscu4nLFUQw – – – – – – Related Reading

  2.   Rosa Belle Holt. Rugs, Oriental and Occidental, Antique & Modern: a Handbook for Ready Reference. (A.C. McClurg & co., Chicago: 1908.)
  3. Philip Deloria. Playing Indian.
  4.  Bsumek, Erika Marie. Indian-made: Navajo Culture in the Marketplace, 1868-1940. (University Of Kansas, 2012.)

item.title: Colonizing the Southwest: Capitalism, Assimilation and Americanization
item.dc:creator: alinaisabella
item.content:encoded:
Introduction The focus of this lesson is to discuss the impact of western expansion and manifest destiny on Native peoples in the American Southwest. We will discuss the transformation of Native society on the backdrop of the Dawes Act, the land run, and attempts to populate the Southwest, in addition to the importance of giving voice to those silenced and offering providing accurate contextualization to primary source material. This exercise, students will learn to pose questions of primary source documents by reading and analyzing "Indian Trader" catalogs, and comparing them to oral interviews with Navajo weavers. They conduct research to follow up these questions and use their findings to create an introduction to and annotations for the catalogs and acquisition documents. The larger goal of this exercise is to introduce students to research and the importance to telling the stories of people who are still living and can be impacted by our work. While students are not required to formulate an original thesis, they learn to conduct independent research and synthesize primary and secondary sources.   Objectives
  • Read and transcribe handwritten documents
  • Pose critical research questions about a primary source
  • Question biases and influence of primary source authors
  • Find and evaluate appropriate secondary sources
  • Create well-researched annotations for places, people and terms mentioned in a primary source document
Context Before utilizing the materials on "Woven into History" and trader catalogs, students will be introduced to such narratives as a genre. Using J. B. Moore's catalog as a jumping off point, we will discuss areas of interest relating to our contextual discussion of the result of the colonization of the American Southwest.
Reading & Source Material
Primary Sources
  1. J.B. Moore Catalog
  2. Dawes Act
  3. Chronicling America Newspapers- 1880-1910
 Secondary Sources
  1. “Natural Indians and Identities of Modernity”. Philip Deloria. Playing Indian .
  2. Navajo Statement on Dawes Act
Additional Resources Photographs via loc.gov (ex. “Navajo Indian”) Chronicling America Newspapers Frederic Allen Williams Photographs William S. Soule Photographs Marsha Weisiger, Dreaming of Sheep in Navajo Country (3-30) Erika Bsumek, Indian-Made: Navajo Culture in the Marketplace, 1868-1940
Assignment:
Utilizing the acquisition records, linked trader catalogs and students will be required to think deeply on biases, national identity, and systematic and environmental racism. Part 1: Students will select one section of a trader catalog and one photograph of a weaver and blanket. The latter will serve as the inspiration for this project.
  • an introduction to the trader catalog providing relevant contextual information, a summary, and annotations
Part 2: Using additional primary and secondary information, students will draft an essay with:
  • A description of the textile with an explanation of symbolism and time period
  • Rewriting of “Weaver Profiles” with their voice using oral histories, imaginative questioning, and historical context from the Navajo perspective

item.title: Cultural Definitions: The Whirling Log
item.dc:creator: alinaisabella
item.content:encoded:
It is important to note the difference in cultural definitions of the swastika, especially in regards to the time period in question.

The word swastika comes from the Sanskrit svastika, which means “good fortune” or “well-being." (see "History of the Swastika")

While twentieth-century European representations of the motif have valid negative connotations, 18th and 19th-century North American usages, in a Native American context, have different meanings. See Woven Sampler (2148-589) [gallery type="square" size="large" link="none" ids="326,325"]       [caption id="attachment_753" align="alignnone" width="777"] For information on teaching Native American Symbolism in the Classroom see Wardle, Barbra L. "Native American Symbolism in the Classroom." Art Education 43, no. 5 (1990): 12-24. doi:10.2307/3193243.[/caption]

item.title: The Wild West?: Native Peoples and the Market Revolution
item.dc:creator: alinaisabella
item.content:encoded:
Level: High School/ College Duration: 1-2 Class Periods Subject: Market Revolution, Westward Expansion, Manifest Destiny, Native People and Removal, Misc. 19th Century Themes
Introduction
For this class period students will think critically about sources and museum holdings by humanizing federal legislation. Students will be divided into groups to explore themes mentioned in Give Me Liberty! Map (high school) or select a primary source reading from list (college).  
Tools for Teachers
Common Lit: Manifest Destiny, Resistance to Reservations    Avalon Project Primary Sources: Dawes Act, Homestead Act, Indian Removal Act PBS: Chief Joseph Speech Guidelines for Primary Source Literacy Sample Presentation:  DOWNLOADABLE PDF
Materials
  • History Textbook  
  • Projector
  • Three computers or ipads
  • Printed Worksheets
  • Map based on Give Me Liberty! Resources
[googlemaps https://www.google.com/maps/d/u/0/embed?mid=1-2ZF0lCbc4rof5964_YBmtG3BFj53spA&w=640&h=480]
Objectives
  • Discuss the major legislative events in the 19th century involving Native Americans in the Southwest.
  • Identify and communicate information found in primary sources, including summarizing the content of the source and identifying and reporting key components such as how it was created, by whom, when, and what it is.
  • Situate a primary source in context by applying knowledge about the time and culture in which it was created; the author or creator; its format, genre, publication history; or related materials in a collection.
  • Demonstrate historical empathy, curiosity about the past, and appreciation for historical sources and historical actors.
Class Agenda
  • 15 minutes: Students will watch selected videos on the Market Revolution and Westward Expansion (Foner, Green)
  • 5-10 minutes: Discuss key themes (Westward expansion, railroad, Dawes Act, Homestead Act, Buffalo, Boarding Schools, civilize)
  • 35 minutes: Students will be divided into three groups. Each will read and discuss among themselves one of the themes in the Give Me Liberty map, taking notes on key themes, dates, and events. Students will construct a 2-3 slide presentation (powerpoint, prezi, google slides, etc.)
  • 10-15 minutes:  Two representatives of each group will share with the class the main themes of map
 
Assignment
 
High School
  • Slide 1- Choose Postcard from Woven Into History. Describe it briefly (who is in it, how is it described, how is it relevant to the discussion)
  • Slide 2/3- Outline of main terms with definitions
College
  • Select Primary source reading
    • President Jackson’s speech on Indian Removal (1830)
    • Homestead Act (1862)
    • Dawes Act (1887)
  •  Create Presentation for class to include
    • One image/postcard from Woven Into History
    • Historical context of image including relevance to primary source
    • Main themes of primary source document & significance (5 W’s- Who, what, why, when, where)
Primary Source Reading
 
Excerpt of Chief Joseph Speech [On a visit to Washington, D.C., 1879] “I cannot understand why so many chiefs are allowed to talk so many different ways, and promise so many different things. I have seen the Great Father Chief [President Hayes]; the Next Great Chief [Secretary of the Interior]; the Commissioner Chief; the Law Chief; and many other law chiefs [Congressmen] and they all say they are my friends, and that I shall have justice, but while all their mouths talk right I do not understand why nothing is done for my people. I have heard talk and talk but nothing is done. Good words do not last long unless they amount to something. Words do not pay for my dead people. They do not pay for my country now overrun by white men. They do not protect my father's grave. They do not pay for my horses and cattle. Good words do not give me back my children. Good words will not make good the promise of your war chief, General Miles. Good words will not give my people a home where they can live in peace and take care of themselves. I am tired of talk that comes to nothing. It makes my heart sick when I remember all the good words and all the broken promises. There has been too much talking by men who had no right to talk. Too many misinterpretations have been made; too many misunderstandings have come up between the white men and the Indians. If the white man wants to live in peace with the Indian he can live in peace. There need be no trouble. Treat all men alike. Give them the same laws. Give them all an even chance to live and grow. All men were made by the same Great Spirit Chief. They are all brothers. The earth is the mother of all people, and all people should have equal rights upon it. You might as well expect all rivers to run backward as that any man who was born a free man should be contented penned up and denied liberty to go where he pleases. If you tie a horse to a stake, do you expect he will grow fat? If you pen an Indian up on a small spot of earth and compel him to stay there, he will not be contented nor will he grow and prosper. I have asked some of the Great White Chiefs where they get their authority to say to the Indian that he shall stay in one place, while he sees white men going where they please. They cannot tell me. I only ask of the Government to be treated as all other men are treated. If I cannot go to my own home, let me have a home in a country where my people will not die so fast. I would like to go to Bitter Root Valley. There my people would be happy; where they are now they are dying. Three have died since I left my camp to come to Washington. When I think of our condition, my heart is heavy. I see men of my own race treated as outlaws and driven from country to country, or shot down like animals.”

item.title: Archives in Conversation: Getting the Full Picture
item.dc:creator: alinaisabella
item.content:encoded:
The photo below captures Frederic Allen Williams in his studio in 1940. It is one of many incredible, newly digitized, lantern slides available through a digital project called Frederic Allen Williams: A Citizen Artist with a Magic Lantern. Each of the items in this digitized collection is functionally a part of the collection Williams donated to the University of Texas after his death. While educators and students will find that digital archives can be effective independently, collections that have been separated, like the Williams Collection, are most effective and useful in conversation with other archives. Here is an example. [caption id="attachment_869" align="alignnone" width="700"] "Studio 1940" photo of Frederic Allen Williams by Jesse Ritner. More photos available at fredericallenwilliams.wordpress.com  William's photos can be found in the Harry Ransom Center.[/caption] In 1940, along Frederic Allen William's journey to collect items for his "Horse Museum", he posed for a series of photographs in his studio. One can imagine him positioning most of the items in the room to be symmetric and guide the eye across to each and every one of his "unique" pieces from across the "great" American frontier. Two human-size sculptures stand on either side of the photograph. A belt hangs strategically on the right. Williams sits in the middle of the frame,  on a red, black, creme, and tan Chief's blanket, with what appears to be "The Arrowmaker", sitting beside him. A pillow is placed next to the sculpture.  The rest of the room includes at least 8 other sculptures, a blanket thrown over a table with a vase and bowl placed on it, a hat, and oddly placed leather pants. The pillow on William's right was likely not intended to be a pillow or a bag which it is labeled as in archival storage. It is a composite of two samplers, one side with the design of a cross and the other with a zig-zag diamond and four crosses seemingly cut in half for the post-sale transformation into a bag/pillow. Woven samplers were much smaller than full blankets, scarves, and rugs. They offered traders/collectors the opportunity to see design previews before commissioning an item. For Williams, however,  it was simply a pillow.   [gallery ids="895,896,897,898,899" type="slideshow" link="none"] The Chief's blanket William's is sitting on (below) is one of several on loan to the Blanton Museum of Art. Only half of the blanket is visible but seeing as all Chief's are symmetric, one would still be able to get a decent idea of what the entire textile looks like by solely examining the photograph. It is third phase transitional style, meaning it was likely created between 1880-1890, and contains Germantown dyes. Art archivists described it as follows:
"Three broad red bands separated by two broad cream bands. The red bands have brown and black parallel stripes separated by red. The natural bands have one central stripe of brown and black adjacent stripes. These bands are broken on the edges and center by concentric diamond and half-diamond patterns, which are filled with parallel yellow and black parallel stripes in the outer frame and cream and black stripes within the central frame."
What is lost in Williams' studio portrait is the legacy of appropriating Diné textiles, the exchange of goods between weavers, traders and collectors, and how such pieces of art were transformed to create an Americanized vision of Diné women and people in the Southwest. [caption id="attachment_987" align="aligncenter" width="492"] Chief Blanket (2148-606)[/caption] It is imperative students, educators, and researchers alike, understand the impact of extractive industries, governments, and scholars that promise so much yet under deliver. And more so,  to think critically about the ways in which the biases of others are written into the archive, and how our research, if not done properly can reproduce those biases and stereotypes. The Frederic Allen Williams collection itself has so many layers– how it came together, the collector's wishes for it upon being donated, how archivists understood and consequently cataloged it, the influence of traders, collectors, and outside forces that shaped style (design/pattern, market value, dyes, and fabric) and then the sociopolitical, economic, and historical contexts that shaped each of the individuals that came in contact with these textiles.
